title: Fiction, Falsehoods, and Few Facts: Cross-Sectional Study on the Content-Related Quality of Atopic Eczema-Related Videos on YouTube
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the 100 most viewed atopic eczema videos on YouTube. Videos were classified by dermatologists as useful, misleading or neither against current scientific evidence, and the paper reports the share of items classified misleading (48/100) and the share classified potentially harmful (34/100) with explicit denominators. Explicit misleading coding against expert scientific ground truth meets the CONTENT criterion; the DISCERN/GQS quality-band shares are additionally recorded as a QUALITY row.

estimates.country: United Kingdom (YouTube searched with the filters 'English UK' language and 'United Kingdom' country)
estimates.date: Searched 18 April 2018; videos re-reviewed in detail in August 2018 without changing rankings
estimates.measure_type: % of the 100 most viewed atopic eczema YouTube videos classified as misleading
estimates.denominator: The 100 most viewed atopic eczema videos on YouTube (8,527,624 total views), after excluding videos of poor technical quality, duplicates and non-English videos without English subtitles
estimates.definition: A video containing scientifically unproven or inaccurate information according to currently available scientific evidence (e.g. unfounded claims about pathogenesis, treatment with unproven dietary, herbal or alternative therapy, or negative portrayal of evidence-based treatment)
estimates.misinfo_def: misleading videos had scientifically unproven or inaccurate information according to currently available scientific evidence (eg, unfounded claims about pathogenesis and treatment with unproven dietary, herbal, or alternative therapy or negative portrayal of evidence-based treatment)
estimates.source_quote: Additionally, 32.0% (32/100) of the videos were classified as useful, 48.0% (48/100) were classified as misleading, and 34.0% (34/100) were classified as potentially harmful.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract, Results, p. 1 (restated in the Results section, p. 4: 'Overall, 32.0% (32/100) of the videos were classified as useful, 48.0% (48/100) were classified as misleading, and 20.0% (20/100) were classified as neither nor.')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Seven experienced dermatologists (the authors, excluding ZRM, OF and AN) rated the videos; discrepancies were re-evaluated and arbitrated by the principal investigator. Intraclass correlation coefficients of 0.97 (DISCERN) and 0.95 (GQS) are reported, indicating excellent interrater reliability for the quality instruments; no separate agreement statistic is reported for the useful/misleading classification.
estimates.moderator_quote: YouTube was searched on April 18, 2018, using the term “atopic eczema” with the following filter settings: “English UK” (language), “United Kingdom” (country), and “Video” (type). Thereafter, videos were sorted by view count ... we limited our analysis to the 100 most viewed videos
estimates.notes: Country is coded United Kingdom because the search was explicitly localised to the UK (language 'English UK', country 'United Kingdom'), i.e. the sample is what a UK searcher would see; the videos themselves were uploaded internationally (United States 43%, unknown 14%, India 12%). The corpus is a rank-truncated most-viewed set for a single health topic, hence denom_scope topical with denom_selection curated. The 'misleading' definition is veracity-based (scientifically unproven or inaccurate against current evidence), so this is CONTENT, not QUALITY.

estimates.country: United Kingdom (YouTube searched with the filters 'English UK' language and 'United Kingdom' country)
estimates.date: Searched 18 April 2018; videos re-reviewed in detail in August 2018
estimates.measure_type: % of the 100 most viewed atopic eczema YouTube videos rated of poor scientific quality on the DISCERN/Global Quality Scale instruments
estimates.value_raw: Among the 100 videos, 68.0% (68/100) and 62.0% (62/100) were of poor and very poor scientific quality, respectively
estimates.denominator: The 100 most viewed atopic eczema videos on YouTube
estimates.definition: Videos scoring in the poor bands of the DISCERN instrument (16 questions on reliability, quality of health information and overall quality, 1-5 points each) and of the 5-point Global Quality Scale
estimates.misinfo_def: n/a - these are generic quality instruments, not a definition of misinformation
estimates.source_quote: Among the 100 videos, 68.0% (68/100) and 62.0% (62/100) were of poor and very poor scientific quality, respectively.
estimates.page_loc: Abstract (supported by Figure 1 and by the Discussion: 'only 11.0% (11/100) and 13.0% (13/100) of the videos, respectively, were of good or excellent quality')
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Seven experienced dermatologists applied DISCERN and the Global Quality Scale; intraclass correlation coefficients 0.97 and 0.95 respectively; discrepancies arbitrated by the principal investigator. Mean overall DISCERN 1.99 (SD 1.09) and mean GQS 2.12 (SD 1.09) on 1-5 scales.
estimates.moderator_quote: The two frequently used quality assessments DISCERN (name of the instrument) and Global Quality Scale (GQS) were applied to evaluate the medical quality of the posted videos
estimates.notes: Construct QUALITY per the governing rule (DISCERN/GQS scores are quality instruments, not veracity), so this row is kept but must be excluded from any prevalence estimate. Confidence is low because the abstract sentence is ambiguous: '68.0% ... and 62.0% ... were of poor and very poor scientific quality, respectively' most plausibly means the poor-quality share under each of the two instruments (DISCERN then GQS, the ordering the paper uses elsewhere: 'only 11.0% (11/100) and 13.0% (13/100) of the videos, respectively, were of good or excellent quality' for DISCERN and GQS), but read literally it would mean 68% poor plus 62% very poor, which cannot both hold on 100 videos. The Conclusion's 'two-thirds of the videos analyzed were below acceptable medical quality standards' supports reading 68% as the headline poor-quality share, which is the value recorded.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) the 32.0% useful and 20.0% neither-nor shares — complements of the misleading share; (2) '71% (34/48) were considered potentially harmful' and '29% (14/48) were considered not harmful' — the same counts expressed inside the misleading subsample; the full-sample version (34/100) is the row kept; (3) the harmful-content type breakdown computed inside the 41 nonscientific and potentially harmful videos (37% [15/41] unnecessary diets, 19% [8/41] discrediting conventional medicine, 15% [6/41] unrealistic promises, 17% [7/41] no limits on UV/steroids/antibiotics/cold packs, 7% [3/41] unscientific harmful procedures, 5% [2/41] harmful topical substances) — categories of harmful advice, not falsity shares, and computed within a misinformation-only subsample; (4) '11.0% (11/100) and 13.0% (13/100) ... of good or excellent quality' — the good-quality tail of the same QUALITY distribution already recorded; (5) view counts by category ('misleading videos had 870,012 views, including 789,073 views for potentially dangerous content, whereas useful videos had only 528,352 views, resulting in a misleading/useful video ratio of 1.65') — no view-weighted share of misinformation is stated, and computing one from the total 8,527,624 views is not permitted, especially since the most-viewed video was excluded from the view analysis; (6) upload-source and topic distributions (50% CAM promoters/personal-experience users, 42% therapeutical advertisers, 8% nonprofits/universities, 43% uploaded from the United States) — provenance and topic, not veracity. Uncertainty: the abstract's 'poor and very poor scientific quality' sentence is internally ambiguous (see the QUALITY row's notes), and the country coding rests on the UK search localisation rather than on where the videos originate.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. Search on 18 April 2018 for 'atopic eczema' with filters 'English UK' (language), 'United Kingdom' (country) and 'Video' (type), sorted by view count, restricted to the 100 most viewed videos (8,527,624 views, total duration 7 h 52 min); videos of poor technical quality, duplicates and non-English videos without English subtitles excluded. Videos re-reviewed in August 2018 (categories refined; rankings and numbers unchanged). Seven experienced dermatologists classified each video as useful / misleading / neither nor, with misleading further split into potentially harmful and not harmful, and applied DISCERN (16 items) and the Global Quality Scale (5 points); discrepancies arbitrated by the principal investigator. Interrater reliability: ICC 0.97 (DISCERN) and 0.95 (GQS). Descriptive statistics and Spearman correlations in SPSS 22.0. Author-declared limitations: comments not evaluated, visual design not assessed, snapshot of an arbitrary period, and other quality dimensions (instructional design, educational value) not covered.
rob.item6_quote: videos were classified as “useful” or “misleading,” where useful videos had scientifically correct and accurate information about any aspect of the disease and misleading videos had scientifically unproven or inaccurate information according to currently available scientific evidence (eg, unfounded claims about pathogenesis and treatment with unproven dietary, herbal, or alternative therapy or negative portrayal of evidence-based treatment)
rob.item10_quote: Overall, 32.0% (32/100) of the videos were classified as useful, 48.0% (48/100) were classified as misleading, and 20.0% (20/100) were classified as neither nor.
